name: John the Ripper - Crack Hashes
description: Cracks hashes with John the Ripper. Single mode derives candidates from GECOS/username data in the file and is ideal for Linux passwd entries; wordlist mode runs a dictionary. Review results with --show.
notes: Use --format=<name> when John cannot auto-detect the hash type. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 15 (Password Attacks).

recommended.note: Extract a crackable hash from an SSH key, Office doc, PDF, or ZIP.
GPU-accelerated cracking — faster than JtR for most formats.

examples.label: Inject a custom rule into john.conf then run it (required for --rules=<name>)
examples.command:
# 1. Add [List.Rules:sshRules] header to your rule file:
cat ssh.rule
# [List.Rules:sshRules]
# c $1 $3 $7 $!
# c $1 $3 $7 $@

# 2. Append to john.conf:
sudo sh -c 'cat /home/kali/passwordattacks/ssh.rule >> /etc/john/john.conf'

# 3. Crack using the named rule set:
john --wordlist=ssh.passwords --rules=sshRules ssh.hash

defense.why_it_works: John the Ripper cracks stolen hashes with wordlist, rule, or incremental modes; strong with its jumbo formats and *2john extractors.
defense.prerequisites: Stolen hashes in a supported John format and a wordlist/ruleset.
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1110.002 M1027 Password Policies] Long, high-entropy, unique passwords resist offline cracking; use slow, salted hashing (bcrypt/argon2/PBKDF2) so each guess is expensive. Since the hash is already stolen, the victim cannot detect the cracking - defence is making the hash uncrackable in reasonable time.
defense.misconfiguration: Authentication protocols store or transmit passwords in formats that are offline-crackable: NTLM hashes (no salt, fast GPU attack), NTLMv2 net hashes (slightly slower but crackable), Kerberos RC4 hashes from Kerberoasting (offline crack without network contact), MD5/SHA1 web app hashes (no key stretching). Weak passwords crack in minutes; even complex ones crack with sufficient GPU power if hashing is fast.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# NTLM hash — no salt, instantaneous lookup with rainbow tables:
# Hash: aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:8846f7eaee8fb117ad06bdd830b7586c
# 'password' -> hash computed in microseconds (MD4 algorithm)
# 4x RTX 3090 GPUs: ~300 GH/s NTLM = 8-char complex password cracks in hours

# Web app MD5 password storage:
# $password = md5($_POST['password']);
# Bcrypt would take 1000x longer per attempt for attacker
defense.secure_config:
# Web apps — use bcrypt/Argon2 (adaptive, memory-hard):
import bcrypt
# Hashing:
hashed = bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=12))
# Verification (slow by design):
bcrypt.checkpw(password.encode(), hashed)

# Python — Argon2 (winner of Password Hashing Competition):
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
ph = PasswordHasher(time_cost=3, memory_cost=65536, parallelism=4)
hash = ph.hash(password)
ph.verify(hash, password)
